Below is a synthesis of what “character functional consistency across a video game narrative” means, how it is achieved in practice, how to evaluate it, and where tensions with player agency arise.

# What “functional consistency” means in interactive narratives

Functional consistency refers to keeping a character’s role, goals, beliefs, and behavioral tendencies coherent across time and choices so that their actions remain believable and the story’s consequences feel stable, even as the player intervenes. In many RPGs, morality systems operationalize this by tracking the player character’s alignment and using it to modulate dialogue, alliances, quest availability, and endings, thereby preserving a functional role (e.g., “lawful good” negotiator) despite diverse encounters and player decisions <cite id="161727fa-0">RPGs commonly represent morality computationally (e.g., good vs. evil scales) and modify gameplay and narrative based on alignment; moral actions move a character along a scale and trigger consequences such as changed NPC reactions, available quests, and endings</cite> <cite id="161727fa-1">Bipolar morality scales update a one-dimensional morality value and have consequences for narrative, progression, and NPC interactions, enabling differentiated character development and scalable defaults like additive or reputation-style accumulation</cite>.

However, when mechanics and narrative pull in opposite directions—e.g., the game rewards “gunning down enemies” while the story portrays moral restraint—players experience “ludonarrative dissonance,” a classic failure of functional consistency. Scholars argue that explicit morality systems often privilege ludostrategic experimentation (e.g., save/load testing) over narratological ethics, undermining the perceived consistency of the character’s moral role <cite id="161727fa-2">Critiques of morality systems emphasize two-dimensional/dualistic limits, selective morality, inconsistent rules, and ludonarrative dissonance; gameplay can encourage ludostrategic behavior that circumvents intended ethical dilemmas, and save/load exploitation “kills” decision irreversibility</cite>.

# Mechanisms that enforce functional consistency

1) Morality/alignment as global state
- Role-playing games encode morality as a stateful profile (one or two dimensions) that conditions behavior and story access. Systems can be additive/neutralizing or accumulate reputation, and many games map ranges to scripted policies (e.g., an NPC arrests when alignment < 0), maintaining a coherent functional role across encounters <cite id="161727fa-1">Bipolar scales implement one-dimensional morality updated by actions, with consequences for quest availability, NPC interactions, and endings; ranges can be mapped to programmed behaviors like arrests</cite>.
- Case study: BioWare’s Mass Effect uses two morality meters (“Paragon”/“Renegade”) whose values carry forward across installments, shaping team dynamics, mission structures, and narrative outcomes; Paragon-leaning play often yields stronger teammate bonds and narrative rewards, illustrating how alignment both scaffolds and constrains choices <cite id="2324befb-2">Mass Effect records and evaluates morality via paragon/renegade meters and transfers moral behavior across three interconnected games, creating interlinked narratological and ludological unity</cite> <cite id="2324befb-3">Paragon choices often build necessary bonds and loyalty; Renegade wipes can also succeed but may miss narrative prerequisites, revealing how the karma system frames and narrows options</cite> <cite id="2324befb-4">Despite attempts to move beyond binary morality, the two-value system imposes a contradictory spectrum and shapes narrative structures, with stronger effects for leaning paragon/renegade</cite>.
- Limits: binary or bipolar scales can compress moral space and produce unintended consequences; designers sometimes embed hidden nudges toward one axis, producing drift and inconsistency complaints from players <cite id="161727fa-2">Critiques emphasize inconsistency and selective morality in explicit systems</cite> <cite id="2324befb-4">Binary presentation of options can contradict intended moral dilemmas and reinforce caricatured spectra</cite>.

2) Agent-based behavior, goals, and organization
- Goal-oriented architectures (e.g., GOAP) and agent organizations model characters as proactively pursuing beliefs, norms, and roles, enabling behavior that adapts to goals and social structures rather than reacting to surface conditions. Commercial uses (F.E.A.R., Deus Ex) and research frameworks (Pogamut, Gamebots) demonstrate how agent organizations provide believable, coherent coordination and adaptation that sustain role consistency under dynamic scenarios <cite id="304e2b54-4">Agent-centered approaches like GOAP control autonomous character behavior in games (e.g., F.E.A.R., Deus Ex), and organizational MAS frameworks (cOncienS/ALIVE) let developers model social structures via norms, roles, and ontologies to build believable, immersive scenarios</cite>.
- These organizational tools can be inverted to make players the “agent” whose goals and norms must remain coherent with a world of roles and duties, supporting the “player as designer of organizations” perspective where character organizations persist and constrain behavior, preserving functional roles across long campaigns <cite id="304e2b54-4">Organization-centered MAS can be used to maintain believable and immersive interactions by modeling norms, roles, and their enactment, and can serve as gameplay interfaces that preserve coherent organizational structures</cite>.

3) Ontologies and knowledge graphs for character models
- Formal ontologies (e.g., event/world taxonomies) and knowledge graphs encode character depth—background, motivation, psychology—along with narrative kernels and expansions, allowing authors to constrain character interaction to consistent roles and functions across branching paths. This supports reuse and authoring while preserving coherence of “necessary story functions” and avoiding ad hoc rule sprawl <cite id="304e2b54-0">LNVM distinguishes world and events ontologies (taxonomies) that encode kernels/nuclei—cardinal functions necessary and sufficient for a story—separable from optional expansions, enabling structured, comparable evaluation of narrative coherence via game- and author-agency over ontologies</cite> <cite id="304e2b54-1">Semantic enrichment via a Game Character Ontology allows structured extraction and reuse of character information from social media, making it usable for games and enabling inference of valid interactions and roles</cite> <cite id="304e2b54-2">Semantically-enriched character knowledge graphs can be constructed to generate complete character models and guide interactions, supporting generation and management without laborious per-entity annotations</cite>.
- In authoring tools, such ontologies can be used to check that a proposed player choice is compatible with a character’s role set and the narrative’s required functions before committing it to world state, reducing inconsistency “bugs” in long-form narratives <cite id="304e2b54-0">Character, world, and event ontologies can be characterized and compared to isolate which degrees of game- and author-agency over narrative kernels and expansions successfully achieve the game’s goals</cite>.

4) Memory-centric persona frameworks for consistency and coherence
- Generative-agent style architectures maintain persona consistency by storing beliefs, traits, and episodic memory that inform perception and action, enabling adaptive yet coherent behavior over time. In interactive storytelling, sustaining believability requires architectures that preserve persona traits while also aligning with the author’s storyline; a useful principle is to jointly optimize persona-consistency with narrative coherence, since purely persona-driven behavior can clash with plot logic and vice versa <cite id="304e2b54-3">Believable characters need lifelike behaviors, autonomous decision-making, and natural responses; persona consistency is maintained via memory-based perception, storage, and retrieval (generative agents). To preserve narrative logic, persona consistency must be balanced with narrative coherence—optimizing both jointly avoids conflicts where a “travel-lover” protagonist fails a “study for exam” arc</cite>.

# Case studies: alignment-driven consistency and its pitfalls

- Mass Effect’s Paragon/Renegade system shows how persistent alignment states can unify a trilogy’s narrative and mechanics, but also how binary constraints can “impose” a moral spectrum and narrow meaningful branching. Empirically, leaning toward one axis yields stronger narrative rewards (e.g., companion loyalty), nudging players toward caricatured roles and producing drift away from truly neutral strategies <cite id="2324befb-2">Moral behavior is recorded and carried across three games, creating a coherent, interlinked ludological-narratological unity</cite> <cite id="2324befb-3">Paragon options often build necessary bonds; Renegade may succeed yet miss prerequisites, illustrating alignment-shaped narrative structures</cite> <cite id="2324befb-4">Two-value morality narrows choices and imposes contradictory spectra, with stronger effects for leaning paragon/renegade</cite>.
- Dragon Age: Origins and Mass Effect 2 illustrate how non-player characters can carry progression and preserve coherence when player-as-protagonist models strain under complex choice spaces. Analyses argue that distributing narrative agency across richly motivated NPCs can maintain coherence more reliably than solely relying on a player-character whose goals and constraints are hard to encode exhaustively <cite id="2324befb-0">Comparative analysis of Dragon Age: Origins and Mass Effect 2 argues that letting non-player characters carry the weight of narrative progression can better establish and maintain narrative coherence</cite>.
- Planescape: Torment offers a counterexample: a multidimensional alignment matrix that dynamically updates from decisions, mapping distinct alignments to unique story and item consequences. Its text-first design makes multidimensional consistency tractable by tightly coupling narrative conditions to alignment checks, contrasting with binary systems that compress moral space <cite id="2324befb-4">Planescape: Torment mixes dynamic moral systems with static alignment matrices; every alignment yields unique story and item consequences, made feasible by primarily text-driven storytelling</cite>.

# Evaluating functional consistency over time

Direct authoring tools can help pre-validate consistency by checking whether proposed narrative events preserve alignment/role constraints. For example, systems that model event kernels and expansions allow authors to test if a choice or event is compatible with character ontologies and alignment thresholds before deployment, improving predictability across branches <cite id="304e2b54-0">Event ontologies distinguish necessary kernels from optional expansions, enabling systematic checks of whether game- and author-agency over ontologies maintain coherent story functions</cite>. 

At runtime, two orthogonal checks can expose inconsistency:
- Persona/role validity: Does the character’s internal state (beliefs, roles, norms) permit the observed action? Memory-centric agents expose violations when a character would “surprise” itself (e.g., a pacifist hero suddenly executes), indicating drift from intended persona <cite id="304e2b54-3">Memory-based architectures preserve persona consistency by constraining perceptions and actions to stored beliefs, making it possible to detect when behaviors violate a character’s persona</cite>.
- Narrative coherence: Does a choice disrupt plot logic or break prior commitments? Joint optimization of persona and narrative coherence helps catch conflicts where a character’s trait makes an action implausible within the story’s current stage (e.g., a traveler refusing to road-trip during an exam arc) <cite id="304e2b54-3">Narrative coherence requires aligning character activities with the author’s storyline; conflicts between persona-consistent behavior and plot logic must be resolved by jointly considering both constraints</cite>.

Practical playtesting metrics include:
- Alignment drift rate: The change in a character’s moral axis between intended and emergent outcomes across decision points.
- NPC reaction fidelity: Proportion of responses that match baseline alignment-conditioned behavior for their faction/relationship band.
- Choice compatibility score: Fraction of player decisions that are acceptable under the character’s current persona/alignment without narrative reset or ad hoc rule override <cite id="161727fa-1">Alignment-based consequences for NPC interactions and quest availability provide measurable axes for evaluating whether choices remain compatible with a character’s moral state</cite> <cite id="2324befb-2">Transferring morality across installments in Mass Effect creates a measurable long-form consistency test case</cite>.

# Trade-offs: player agency, emergent behavior, and repair strategies

Player agency creates “wicked problems” for consistency: moral dilemmas can be solved by brute-force experimentation (save/load), eroding the perceived integrity of a moral role and producing dissonance between what the story demands and what mechanics allow <cite id="161727fa-2">Wicked problems include selective and inconsistent rule systems and ludonarrative dissonance; players can exploit save/load to try all options, undermining decision gravity</cite>. Agent organizations and norms can help: by embedding norms and roles into the system, characters’ reactions and offers remain coherent even when the player deviates, because the world’s social fabric persists and constrains behavior <cite id="304e2b54-4">Organizational frameworks encode norms and roles in ontologies and provide agent interfaces to game engines, enabling believable, coherent behavior and adaptation</cite>.

When inconsistency emerges, repair strategies include:
- Adaptive filtering of choices: hide or reframe options that would violate a character’s current persona/alignment, or present them as socially risky, thereby preserving the role without hard rewrites <cite id="304e2b54-3">Maintaining persona consistency through memory-based perception and retrieval enables adaptive yet coherent behavior, supporting runtime filtering to avoid incompatible actions</cite>.
- Narrative patching with lightweight author checks: before committing a choice, run ontology-level coherence checks against character role sets and event kernels; if incoherent, either reject the branch, present a consequence-clarifying prompt, or apply a minimal state update (e.g., reputation shift) to restore equilibrium <cite id="304e2b54-0">Ontology-based categorization of world and event taxonomies supports efficient strategies for comparable evaluation and design, enabling checks that preserve story kernels under author agency</cite>.
- Long-form alignment scaffolding: use multi-dimensional morality or reputation-like profiles to avoid binary collapse, making it possible to preserve nuanced roles (e.g., “lawful neutral with strong diplomatic ties”) that survive partial deviations <cite id="2324befb-4">Mass Effect’s binary system imposes contradictions, whereas multidimensional alignment (as in Planescape: Torment) yields unique, role-preserving consequences per alignment</cite>.

# A practical blueprint

- Choose a consistency substrate:
  - For RPG-style morality, start with a multi-dimensional or reputation-like profile; encode moral/legality axes with range-to-policy mappings for NPCs and quests, and persist across saves/load/sequels <cite id="161727fa-1">Bipolar scales can be additive or reputation-style and map ranges to behaviors like arrests</cite> <cite id="2324befb-2">Mass Effect carries paragon/renegade meters across installments to unify story and mechanics</cite> <cite id="2324befb-4">Multidimensional alignment yields unique story and item consequences per alignment</cite>.
  - For social organizations, model factions, norms, and roles with an organizational MAS; equip agents with goals and norms to react coherently to state changes and maintain believable coordination <cite id="304e2b54-4">Organizational MAS (cOncienS/ALIVE) provide ontologies for norms, roles, and behaviors to build believable systems</cite>.
- Author with ontologies:
  - Define character ontologies (traits, goals, relationships) and event ontologies (kernels and expansions); use them to pre-validate that proposed branches and dialog options preserve role coherence and story kernels <cite id="304e2b54-0">Event kernels and expansions allow structured, comparable evaluation of narrative coherence via ontologies</cite> <cite id="304e2b54-1">Game Character Ontologies extract and annotate character information to support coherent interaction semantics</cite>.
- Run dual monitors at runtime:
  - Persona monitor: track belief/perception consistency via memory traces; raise soft constraints (filtering) or hard rejections (override with minimal state changes) when violations occur <cite id="304e2b54-3">Memory-based architectures sustain persona consistency; conflicts between persona and plot are resolved by jointly optimizing both</cite>.
  - Coherence monitor: check that current choices align with story-stage expectations and prior commitments; use alignment constraints and role sets to predict and mitigate dissonance <cite id="161727fa-1">Alignment has consequences for available quests, rewards, and NPC interactions, enabling measurable checks</cite>.
- Test and iterate:
  - Playtest for alignment drift and NPC reaction fidelity; instrument logs to compute compatibility scores and drift rates across decision trees; iteratively prune or reweight branches that systematically violate role/plot coherence <cite id="304e2b54-0">Ontology-guided analysis supports efficient design and evaluation strategies for narrative coherence</cite>.

# Open challenges

- Balancing agency and coherence: save/load exploitation and moral override mechanics can defeat intended consistency; designers must embed irreversible stakes or pacing that preserves moral gravity without punishing experimentation <cite id="161727fa-2">Save/load exploitation undermines ethical gameplay and decision irreversibility</cite>.
- Richer semantics: moving beyond binary scales without exploding production cost; multidimensional systems require principled synthesis and scalable authoring tools <cite id="2324befb-4">Binary systems impose contradictory spectra; multidimensional alignment yields unique consequences but raises production complexity</cite>.
- Automated repair: lightweight “plausible choice filters” and ontology-grounded runtime validators can reduce hotfixes, but require robust memory models and cross-domain ontologies to avoid new forms of brittleness <cite id="304e2b54-3">Joint optimization of persona and narrative coherence is needed to prevent conflicts where trait-driven behavior contradicts plot logic</cite>.

In sum, functional consistency is best approached as a layered system: persistent, semantically rich character models (morality/roles/norms) enforced by agent/ontology abstractions, validated by pre-runtime checks and runtime monitors, and tuned through playtesting to honor both the character’s function and the story’s logic. Case-driven evidence from RPGs shows both the promise of alignment scaffolding and the pitfalls of binary reduction; agent- and ontology-based methods provide concrete toolkits for maintaining coherence under player agency, with evaluation centered on role fidelity, narrative compatibility, and long-form stability <cite id="161727fa-0">Morality systems position characters on good/evil scales and modify narrative and gameplay accordingly</cite> <cite id="161727fa-1">Alignment scales update with actions and condition narrative and interactions, enabling scalable consistency</cite> <cite id="161727fa-2">Ludonarrative dissonance and save/load exploitation reveal limits of simplistic systems</cite> <cite id="2324befb-2">Mass Effect’s metered morality unifies a trilogy’s narrative and mechanics</cite> <cite id="304e2b54-4">Agent organizations with norms/roles yield believable, coherent behaviors and coordination</cite> <cite id="304e2b54-3">Memory-centric persona frameworks sustain coherence and can be coupled with narrative constraints for author-intent alignment</cite>.

Snippet: Role-playing games (RPGs) are a genre of videogame in which the player takes on the role of a character or group of characters and plays out a story in a virtual world. In addition to forming a core part of the game mechanics of many RPGs, these representations of morality can be used to pose dilemmas in which the player must choose a course of action (Zagal, 2009;Sicart, 2013). Title: Enduring Design Challenges in Western Roleplaying Video Games
Snippet: Dungeons and Dragons table-top games are the foundation of many RPG's structure and content, including morality mechanics (Tresca, 2010). Advanced Dungeons and Dragons (1979) divided morality into two-dimensions, each with three levels (Figure 5). The morality scale represents concern for others versus selfishness. The legality scale represents respect or contempt for law and order. For example, a chaotic good character might break the law to help someone in need, while a lawful evil character might use the rules to exploit the vulnerable. Many WRPGs contrastingly employ simple, one-dimensional, bipolar morality scales. 

We define a bipolar morality scale as a game mechanic where: 

1. in-game morality is implemented as a one-dimensional spectrum 2. in-game actions move the player toward one end or the other 3. the player character's position on the spectrum has consequences for the game narrative, character progression or in-game events 

In some games, including Fallout 3 (2008), moral actions are additive such that good actions effectively erase evil actions and vice versa. In these games, the player character typically starts in the middle of the spectrum (neutral). In other games, including Mass Effect series, moral actions make permanent contributions to reputation. In these games, the player character typically starts with no reputation and builds up fame or infamy as shown in Figure 4. Table 5 gives examples of bipolar morality scales in some well-known WRPGs. Morality scales are also common in sandbox games such as the Infamous and Far Cry series. Morality scales may be used as game mechanics or narrative mechanics (Ralph & Monu, 2015). The player's morality score may affect numerous aspects of the game including: 

• abilities the player can learn • bonuses the player receives • available quests and rewards • random encounters • a character's appearance • available game endings and epilogues • available NPC interactions, including dialogue options and which NPCs will join the player's party Bipolar morality scales are attractive because they limit the complexity of programmed responses. For example, given a scale from -1000 (chaotic) to +1000 (lawful), a sheriff NPC might be programmed to attempt an arrest for any score less than 0, and do nothing otherwise.

While morality systems are a well-established game mechanic, they have come under criticism from academic scholars (Knoll, 2014;Nguyen, 2016;Sicart, 2013a;Svelch, 2010;Zagal, 2009) and game critics alike (Birch, 2014;Rio, 2014;Takacs, 2013). The criticisms focus on the two-dimensional (dualistic) nature of the systems, their selective morality, the inconsistency of the rule systems, and the notion of "ludonarrative dissonance" (Hocking, 2007). Especially the last criticism is important with regard to ethical gameplay. If in any given game, the game's narrative conflicts with its mechanics, the ethical gameplay is disturbed because the player experiences a divide between what the game seems to ask from the player (moral behavior) and what the game actually makes the player do (gunning down hordes of enemies). Of course, this could be intended as such by the game developers as some sort of meta-ethical discussion, but it hardly ever is. 

As Sicart (2013a) has mentioned, the problem with many morality systems (especially the explicit ones) is that the gameplay actually encourages ludostrategic behavior in gamers instead of the required narratological-ethical behavior (Knoll, 2014). This means that players are more inclined to look for the biggest advantage in terms of gameplay and to disregard the morally charged game narrative. Sicart (2013a) has also argued that most moral dilemmas in video games can be easily circumvented by experimenting (exploiting) the load/save system of the game. It is quite possible, especially in cases that have only short-term consequences, to literally try all possible options in any given dilemma until the best result is achieved. This of course "kills" the most important aspect of ethical gameplay, that is, the decision is one-off and irreversible.

Title: Outlining a Serious Moral Games in Bioethics
Snippet: Up to recently, the general relationship between morality and video games was considered from a limited perspective. It was (and is) common to debate whether certain games (such as first-person shooters) have a negative impact on the moral development of adolescents [8], although the findings are controversial [9]. 

We will not comment on this debate here, but we remark that an increasing interest in creating "pro-social" video games has shown up in several ways. Some authors strongly maintain that video games -in contrast to other instruments of moral education like stories or films -are particularly well suited for such purposes in that such games do not merely convey content; rather, the rules on which the games are based allow the player to act (within the established framework of the game) [10], and thus interact, rather than simply absorb. This use of video games is accompanied by a noteworthy development in the game industry. There have been for some time games on the market in which the player has to develop explicitly moral qualities (e.g. cooperation) to succeed. The associated "socially conscious artificial intelligence" aspect of a game engine has become quite common in game design. Examples of such behaviours include taking responsibility or feeling empathy for game characters, and a game flow that responds to the behaviour of the players (e.g. assertive versus cautious) [11]. However, the possibility of moral decisions in such games is not usually discussed in terms of their possible realization in a video game, but in the context of cultural analysis [12]. 

Nevertheless, this discussion points to the possibility of creating a SMG: a game that enables one to determine the "morality" of players, and possibly have an effect on their behaviour outside of the game world as well. 1. What does one mean by the idea of "morality"? In a general sense, "morality" describes the social norms and values that constitute the standard for "morally correct behaviour". Moreover, the representation of semantically-enriched and semantically -interlinked game character content would enable game character generators or game character asset managers to infer how characters can be interacted within the game world without having to rely on software development procedures that require laborious annotation of how each entity can be interacted within the game. 

In this paper, we present our framework to extract video game character content from social media platforms, such as from wiki-based systems --e.g. Fandom [4] and Giant Bomb [5]. The extracted character content is semantically annotated using our Game Character Ontology (GCO) [36] -a light-weight vocabulary for describing character information in video games. The remainder of this paper is as follows: Section 2 provides use case scenarios for using extracted character information. Section 3 reviews current work on semantics in games, existing game ontologies for describing character information, and methodologies for extracting and semantic-annotating text. Section 4 offers core background information about the Web of data. In Section 5 we discuss the type of game content available in social media platforms from which character information can be extracted. This section also provides an overview of our Game Character Ontology (GCO) and provides some examples for describing game character content using GCO. Section 6 provides our methodology for extracting and semantically annotating content from social media platforms using GCO, and section 7 provides preliminary results of the extraction methodology. Section 8 concludes the paper by providing an overall discussion about the future steps of our work.

Title: Extracting Semantic-Based Video Game Characters Information from Social Media Platforms
Snippet: Character generation in video games currently relies on game developers manually creating game characters which costs in time, effort and resources. Social media, in the form of blogs, microblogs, forums, wikis, social networks and review sites contain rich information about characters in video games that are not exploited for character generation. However, such information contained in various social media applications are disconnected from one another and are not structured or enriched that can be utilised for character generation. Semantic Web techniques provide ways of linking and enriching information contained in disconnected datasets. This enriched information can be used to build complete character models for generating new characters in video games. Moreover, a video game character knowledge graph can be constructed out of the semantically-enriched information that can be used not only for character generation in video games, but also in any application that requires information about video game characters. In this paper, we present our approach for exploiting social media platforms to create semantically-enriched character models. In particular, we present our Game Character Ontology (GCO) – a light-weight vocabulary for describing character information in video games – and our methodology for extracting and describing (using our ontology) game character information from social media platforms.

Title: DiaryPlay: AI-Assisted Creation of Interactive Story Vignettes for Everyday Storytelling
Snippet: Virtual characters (e.g., AI agents [65]) are designed to interact with users and simulate real-life behaviors in interactive digital storytelling. To create engaging and immersive experiences, believability has been set as a central design goal [65], meaning characters should exhibit lifelike behaviors, make decisions autonomously, and respond naturally to evolving scenarios [7,89]. A well-defined persona is essential for believable characters [2,48,52]. Beyond traditional attribute-based specification, recent work explores conversation-based persona construction in which authors build characters through dialogue with an LLM to better finetune its persona [74]. Commercial tools (e.g., CharacterAI [60]) similarly let users define descriptions, greetings, example dialogues, and personality tags, with iterative refinement through response ratings. Beyond initial character construction, sustaining believable interactions requires a character architecture that maintains persona consistency; the generative agent framework [65] addresses this through memory-based perception, storage, and retrieval to support adaptive yet coherent behavior. Beyond making character behaviors consistent with their persons, our work explores characters that remain believable while also aligning with an author's intended storyline [53,97]. 

While existing work primarily focuses on the importance of persona consistency [103], in storytelling, we argue that believable character behaviors should also ensure the narrative's logical coherence [77]. However, persona consistency and narrative coherence might conflict in a narrative planning [77,98]. For instance, if a character is portrayed as a person who loves traveling and is set in the storyline to "work hard for a final exam" as a future activity, their behavior becomes less believable if they are shown engaging in a "go on a road trip. " Because it might disrupt the logical flow of the narrative, even if their activity remains consistent with their persona. To address this issue, our work proposes a character activity planning approach that considers both the character's persona consistency as well as narrative coherence.

Title: Organizational Gameplay: The Player as Designer of Character Organizations
Snippet: A major challenge faced by game designers is how to incorporate high-level concerns such as flexible and/or social behaviors into the gaming experience. Usually, NPCs are programmed to react to environmental or other character conditions, instead of proactively pursuing explicit goals, be it alone or in collaboration with other characters. Hence, in most cases, their actions do not look natural from the human player perception. 

In an attempt to overcome this limitation some research work have proposed the use of agent centered approaches to control characters. One of the first attempts to connect intelligent agents to games was Gamebots [23]. It provided an infrastructure to allow the connection of any agent platform and the Unreal Tournament game. Gamebots was later used as the base for Pogamut [24], a Java middleware that enables controlling virtual agents (NPCs) in multiple environments provided by game engines. Another noteworthy agent centered work is the GOAP architecture [25]. GOAP is a STRIPSlike planning architecture specifically designed for real-time control of autonomous character behavior in games. It is used in several commercial games such as F.E.A.R and Deus Ex: Human Revolution. 

Regarding the use of organization centered MAS in game design, two relevant works are [26] and cOncienS [27]. In [26], the authors propose the use of agent organizations to control the coordination and adaptation in the context of serious games. Their aim is to adapt the learning experience to the skill level of each trainee, while maintaining the game believable and immersive. cOncienS [27] is a research work based on a larger project called ALIVE which defines an organizational framework to build service-oriented systems. It presents a set of tools for game developers to model scenarios using social structures. Specifically, it provides a programming interface for coupling agents to game engines, a tool for creating organization ontologies (specifications of agent organizations), and elements to describe character behaviors based on norms, roles, and their enactment. 

In comparison, our proposal differs from these earlier works in a main aspect. Our research focuses on the use of organization technology as gaming interface or gameplay.

Title: Game Characters as Narrative Devices. A Comparative Analysis of Dragon Age: Origins and Mass Effect 2
Snippet: This article presents a comparative analysis of how characters are used as narrative tools in Bioware’s computer role-playing games Dragon Age: Origins (2009) and Mass Effect 2 (2010). The analysis aims to demonstrate how sophisticated narrative features can be integrated in gameplay through the development of interesting characters. Using a comparative analysis, the author shows that the two games’ have different approaches to using characters as narrative tools within the same genre, while also incorporating these narrative features tightly into gameplay. Central to the argument is the idea that presenting the player as protagonist is not necessarily the most fruitful approach to narrative experiences in games, and that narrative coherence may be better established and maintained through letting non-player characters carry the weight of narrative progression.

Below is a synthesis of what “character functional consistency across a video game narrative” means, how it is achieved in practice, how to evaluate it, and where tensions with player agency arise.

# What “functional consistency” means in interactive narratives

Functional consistency refers to keeping a character’s role, goals, beliefs, and behavioral tendencies coherent across time and choices so that their actions remain believable and the story’s consequences feel stable, even as the player intervenes. In many RPGs, morality systems operationalize this by tracking the player character’s alignment and using it to modulate dialogue, alliances, quest availability, and endings, thereby preserving a functional role (e.g., “lawful good” negotiator) despite diverse encounters and player decisions <cite id="161727fa-0">RPGs commonly represent morality computationally (e.g., good vs. evil scales) and modify gameplay and narrative based on alignment; moral actions move a character along a scale and trigger consequences such as changed NPC reactions, available quests, and endings</cite> <cite id="161727fa-1">Bipolar morality scales update a one-dimensional morality value and have consequences for narrative, progression, and NPC interactions, enabling differentiated character development and scalable defaults like additive or reputation-style accumulation</cite>.

However, when mechanics and narrative pull in opposite directions—e.g., the game rewards “gunning down enemies” while the story portrays moral restraint—players experience “ludonarrative dissonance,” a classic failure of functional consistency. Scholars argue that explicit morality systems often privilege ludostrategic experimentation (e.g., save/load testing) over narratological ethics, undermining the perceived consistency of the character’s moral role <cite id="161727fa-2">Critiques of morality systems emphasize two-dimensional/dualistic limits, selective morality, inconsistent rules, and ludonarrative dissonance; gameplay can encourage ludostrategic behavior that circumvents intended ethical dilemmas, and save/load exploitation “kills” decision irreversibility</cite>.

# Mechanisms that enforce functional consistency

1) Morality/alignment as global state
- Role-playing games encode morality as a stateful profile (one or two dimensions) that conditions behavior and story access. Systems can be additive/neutralizing or accumulate reputation, and many games map ranges to scripted policies (e.g., an NPC arrests when alignment < 0), maintaining a coherent functional role across encounters <cite id="161727fa-1">Bipolar scales implement one-dimensional morality updated by actions, with consequences for quest availability, NPC interactions, and endings; ranges can be mapped to programmed behaviors like arrests</cite>.
- Case study: BioWare’s Mass Effect uses two morality meters (“Paragon”/“Renegade”) whose values carry forward across installments, shaping team dynamics, mission structures, and narrative outcomes; Paragon-leaning play often yields stronger teammate bonds and narrative rewards, illustrating how alignment both scaffolds and constrains choices <cite id="2324befb-2">Mass Effect records and evaluates morality via paragon/renegade meters and transfers moral behavior across three interconnected games, creating interlinked narratological and ludological unity</cite> <cite id="2324befb-3">Paragon choices often build necessary bonds and loyalty; Renegade wipes can also succeed but may miss narrative prerequisites, revealing how the karma system frames and narrows options</cite> <cite id="2324befb-4">Despite attempts to move beyond binary morality, the two-value system imposes a contradictory spectrum and shapes narrative structures, with stronger effects for leaning paragon/renegade</cite>.
- Limits: binary or bipolar scales can compress moral space and produce unintended consequences; designers sometimes embed hidden nudges toward one axis, producing drift and inconsistency complaints from players <cite id="161727fa-2">Critiques emphasize inconsistency and selective morality in explicit systems</cite> <cite id="2324befb-4">Binary presentation of options can contradict intended moral dilemmas and reinforce caricatured spectra</cite>.

2) Agent-based behavior, goals, and organization
- Goal-oriented architectures (e.g., GOAP) and agent organizations model characters as proactively pursuing beliefs, norms, and roles, enabling behavior that adapts to goals and social structures rather than reacting to surface conditions. Commercial uses (F.E.A.R., Deus Ex) and research frameworks (Pogamut, Gamebots) demonstrate how agent organizations provide believable, coherent coordination and adaptation that sustain role consistency under dynamic scenarios <cite id="304e2b54-4">Agent-centered approaches like GOAP control autonomous character behavior in games (e.g., F.E.A.R., Deus Ex), and organizational MAS frameworks (cOncienS/ALIVE) let developers model social structures via norms, roles, and ontologies to build believable, immersive scenarios</cite>.
- These organizational tools can be inverted to make players the “agent” whose goals and norms must remain coherent with a world of roles and duties, supporting the “player as designer of organizations” perspective where character organizations persist and constrain behavior, preserving functional roles across long campaigns <cite id="304e2b54-4">Organization-centered MAS can be used to maintain believable and immersive interactions by modeling norms, roles, and their enactment, and can serve as gameplay interfaces that preserve coherent organizational structures</cite>.

3) Ontologies and knowledge graphs for character models
- Formal ontologies (e.g., event/world taxonomies) and knowledge graphs encode character depth—background, motivation, psychology—along with narrative kernels and expansions, allowing authors to constrain character interaction to consistent roles and functions across branching paths. This supports reuse and authoring while preserving coherence of “necessary story functions” and avoiding ad hoc rule sprawl <cite id="304e2b54-0">LNVM distinguishes world and events ontologies (taxonomies) that encode kernels/nuclei—cardinal functions necessary and sufficient for a story—separable from optional expansions, enabling structured, comparable evaluation of narrative coherence via game- and author-agency over ontologies</cite> <cite id="304e2b54-1">Semantic enrichment via a Game Character Ontology allows structured extraction and reuse of character information from social media, making it usable for games and enabling inference of valid interactions and roles</cite> <cite id="304e2b54-2">Semantically-enriched character knowledge graphs can be constructed to generate complete character models and guide interactions, supporting generation and management without laborious per-entity annotations</cite>.
- In authoring tools, such ontologies can be used to check that a proposed player choice is compatible with a character’s role set and the narrative’s required functions before committing it to world state, reducing inconsistency “bugs” in long-form narratives <cite id="304e2b54-0">Character, world, and event ontologies can be characterized and compared to isolate which degrees of game- and author-agency over narrative kernels and expansions successfully achieve the game’s goals</cite>.

4) Memory-centric persona frameworks for consistency and coherence
- Generative-agent style architectures maintain persona consistency by storing beliefs, traits, and episodic memory that inform perception and action, enabling adaptive yet coherent behavior over time. In interactive storytelling, sustaining believability requires architectures that preserve persona traits while also aligning with the author’s storyline; a useful principle is to jointly optimize persona-consistency with narrative coherence, since purely persona-driven behavior can clash with plot logic and vice versa <cite id="304e2b54-3">Believable characters need lifelike behaviors, autonomous decision-making, and natural responses; persona consistency is maintained via memory-based perception, storage, and retrieval (generative agents). To preserve narrative logic, persona consistency must be balanced with narrative coherence—optimizing both jointly avoids conflicts where a “travel-lover” protagonist fails a “study for exam” arc</cite>.

# Case studies: alignment-driven consistency and its pitfalls

- Mass Effect’s Paragon/Renegade system shows how persistent alignment states can unify a trilogy’s narrative and mechanics, but also how binary constraints can “impose” a moral spectrum and narrow meaningful branching. Empirically, leaning toward one axis yields stronger narrative rewards (e.g., companion loyalty), nudging players toward caricatured roles and producing drift away from truly neutral strategies <cite id="2324befb-2">Moral behavior is recorded and carried across three games, creating a coherent, interlinked ludological-narratological unity</cite> <cite id="2324befb-3">Paragon options often build necessary bonds; Renegade may succeed yet miss prerequisites, illustrating alignment-shaped narrative structures</cite> <cite id="2324befb-4">Two-value morality narrows choices and imposes contradictory spectra, with stronger effects for leaning paragon/renegade</cite>.
- Dragon Age: Origins and Mass Effect 2 illustrate how non-player characters can carry progression and preserve coherence when player-as-protagonist models strain under complex choice spaces. Analyses argue that distributing narrative agency across richly motivated NPCs can maintain coherence more reliably than solely relying on a player-character whose goals and constraints are hard to encode exhaustively <cite id="2324befb-0">Comparative analysis of Dragon Age: Origins and Mass Effect 2 argues that letting non-player characters carry the weight of narrative progression can better establish and maintain narrative coherence</cite>.
- Planescape: Torment offers a counterexample: a multidimensional alignment matrix that dynamically updates from decisions, mapping distinct alignments to unique story and item consequences. Its text-first design makes multidimensional consistency tractable by tightly coupling narrative conditions to alignment checks, contrasting with binary systems that compress moral space <cite id="2324befb-4">Planescape: Torment mixes dynamic moral systems with static alignment matrices; every alignment yields unique story and item consequences, made feasible by primarily text-driven storytelling</cite>.

# Evaluating functional consistency over time

Direct authoring tools can help pre-validate consistency by checking whether proposed narrative events preserve alignment/role constraints. For example, systems that model event kernels and expansions allow authors to test if a choice or event is compatible with character ontologies and alignment thresholds before deployment, improving predictability across branches <cite id="304e2b54-0">Event ontologies distinguish necessary kernels from optional expansions, enabling systematic checks of whether game- and author-agency over ontologies maintain coherent story functions</cite>. 

At runtime, two orthogonal checks can expose inconsistency:
- Persona/role validity: Does the character’s internal state (beliefs, roles, norms) permit the observed action? Memory-centric agents expose violations when a character would “surprise” itself (e.g., a pacifist hero suddenly executes), indicating drift from intended persona <cite id="304e2b54-3">Memory-based architectures preserve persona consistency by constraining perceptions and actions to stored beliefs, making it possible to detect when behaviors violate a character’s persona</cite>.
- Narrative coherence: Does a choice disrupt plot logic or break prior commitments? Joint optimization of persona and narrative coherence helps catch conflicts where a character’s trait makes an action implausible within the story’s current stage (e.g., a traveler refusing to road-trip during an exam arc) <cite id="304e2b54-3">Narrative coherence requires aligning character activities with the author’s storyline; conflicts between persona-consistent behavior and plot logic must be resolved by jointly considering both constraints</cite>.

Practical playtesting metrics include:
- Alignment drift rate: The change in a character’s moral axis between intended and emergent outcomes across decision points.
- NPC reaction fidelity: Proportion of responses that match baseline alignment-conditioned behavior for their faction/relationship band.
- Choice compatibility score: Fraction of player decisions that are acceptable under the character’s current persona/alignment without narrative reset or ad hoc rule override <cite id="161727fa-1">Alignment-based consequences for NPC interactions and quest availability provide measurable axes for evaluating whether choices remain compatible with a character’s moral state</cite> <cite id="2324befb-2">Transferring morality across installments in Mass Effect creates a measurable long-form consistency test case</cite>.

# Trade-offs: player agency, emergent behavior, and repair strategies

Player agency creates “wicked problems” for consistency: moral dilemmas can be solved by brute-force experimentation (save/load), eroding the perceived integrity of a moral role and producing dissonance between what the story demands and what mechanics allow <cite id="161727fa-2">Wicked problems include selective and inconsistent rule systems and ludonarrative dissonance; players can exploit save/load to try all options, undermining decision gravity</cite>. Agent organizations and norms can help: by embedding norms and roles into the system, characters’ reactions and offers remain coherent even when the player deviates, because the world’s social fabric persists and constrains behavior <cite id="304e2b54-4">Organizational frameworks encode norms and roles in ontologies and provide agent interfaces to game engines, enabling believable, coherent behavior and adaptation</cite>.

When inconsistency emerges, repair strategies include:
- Adaptive filtering of choices: hide or reframe options that would violate a character’s current persona/alignment, or present them as socially risky, thereby preserving the role without hard rewrites <cite id="304e2b54-3">Maintaining persona consistency through memory-based perception and retrieval enables adaptive yet coherent behavior, supporting runtime filtering to avoid incompatible actions</cite>.
- Narrative patching with lightweight author checks: before committing a choice, run ontology-level coherence checks against character role sets and event kernels; if incoherent, either reject the branch, present a consequence-clarifying prompt, or apply a minimal state update (e.g., reputation shift) to restore equilibrium <cite id="304e2b54-0">Ontology-based categorization of world and event taxonomies supports efficient strategies for comparable evaluation and design, enabling checks that preserve story kernels under author agency</cite>.
- Long-form alignment scaffolding: use multi-dimensional morality or reputation-like profiles to avoid binary collapse, making it possible to preserve nuanced roles (e.g., “lawful neutral with strong diplomatic ties”) that survive partial deviations <cite id="2324befb-4">Mass Effect’s binary system imposes contradictions, whereas multidimensional alignment (as in Planescape: Torment) yields unique, role-preserving consequences per alignment</cite>.

# A practical blueprint

- Choose a consistency substrate:
  - For RPG-style morality, start with a multi-dimensional or reputation-like profile; encode moral/legality axes with range-to-policy mappings for NPCs and quests, and persist across saves/load/sequels <cite id="161727fa-1">Bipolar scales can be additive or reputation-style and map ranges to behaviors like arrests</cite> <cite id="2324befb-2">Mass Effect carries paragon/renegade meters across installments to unify story and mechanics</cite> <cite id="2324befb-4">Multidimensional alignment yields unique story and item consequences per alignment</cite>.
  - For social organizations, model factions, norms, and roles with an organizational MAS; equip agents with goals and norms to react coherently to state changes and maintain believable coordination <cite id="304e2b54-4">Organizational MAS (cOncienS/ALIVE) provide ontologies for norms, roles, and behaviors to build believable systems</cite>.
- Author with ontologies:
  - Define character ontologies (traits, goals, relationships) and event ontologies (kernels and expansions); use them to pre-validate that proposed branches and dialog options preserve role coherence and story kernels <cite id="304e2b54-0">Event kernels and expansions allow structured, comparable evaluation of narrative coherence via ontologies</cite> <cite id="304e2b54-1">Game Character Ontologies extract and annotate character information to support coherent interaction semantics</cite>.
- Run dual monitors at runtime:
  - Persona monitor: track belief/perception consistency via memory traces; raise soft constraints (filtering) or hard rejections (override with minimal state changes) when violations occur <cite id="304e2b54-3">Memory-based architectures sustain persona consistency; conflicts between persona and plot are resolved by jointly optimizing both</cite>.
  - Coherence monitor: check that current choices align with story-stage expectations and prior commitments; use alignment constraints and role sets to predict and mitigate dissonance <cite id="161727fa-1">Alignment has consequences for available quests, rewards, and NPC interactions, enabling measurable checks</cite>.
- Test and iterate:
  - Playtest for alignment drift and NPC reaction fidelity; instrument logs to compute compatibility scores and drift rates across decision trees; iteratively prune or reweight branches that systematically violate role/plot coherence <cite id="304e2b54-0">Ontology-guided analysis supports efficient design and evaluation strategies for narrative coherence</cite>.

# Open challenges

- Balancing agency and coherence: save/load exploitation and moral override mechanics can defeat intended consistency; designers must embed irreversible stakes or pacing that preserves moral gravity without punishing experimentation <cite id="161727fa-2">Save/load exploitation undermines ethical gameplay and decision irreversibility</cite>.
- Richer semantics: moving beyond binary scales without exploding production cost; multidimensional systems require principled synthesis and scalable authoring tools <cite id="2324befb-4">Binary systems impose contradictory spectra; multidimensional alignment yields unique consequences but raises production complexity</cite>.

Title: Enduring Design Challenges in Western Roleplaying Video Games

Many WRPGs contrastingly employ simple, one-dimensional, bipolar morality scales. 

We define a bipolar morality scale as a game mechanic where: 

1. in-game morality is implemented as a one-dimensional spectrum 2. in-game actions move the player toward one end or the other 3. the player character's position on the spectrum has consequences for the game narrative, character progression or in-game events

In these games, the player character typically starts in the middle of the spectrum (neutral). In other games, including Mass Effect series, moral actions make permanent contributions to reputation. The criticisms focus on the two-dimensional (dualistic) nature of the systems, their selective morality, the inconsistency of the rule systems, and the notion of "ludonarrative dissonance" (Hocking, 2007). Especially the last criticism is important with regard to ethical gameplay. If in any given game, the game's narrative conflicts with its mechanics, the ethical gameplay is disturbed because the player experiences a divide between what the game seems to ask from the player (moral behavior) and what the game actually makes the player do (gunning down hordes of enemies). Of course, this could be intended as such by the game developers as some sort of meta-ethical discussion, but it hardly ever is. 

As Sicart (2013a) has mentioned, the problem with many morality systems (especially the explicit ones) is that the gameplay actually encourages ludostrategic behavior in gamers instead of the required narratological-ethical behavior (Knoll, 2014). This means that players are more inclined to look for the biggest advantage in terms of gameplay and to disregard the morally charged game narrative. Sicart (2013a) has also argued that most moral dilemmas in video games can be easily circumvented by experimenting (exploiting) the load/save system of the game. It is quite possible, especially in cases that have only short-term consequences, to literally try all possible options in any given dilemma until the best result is achieved. This of course "kills" the most important aspect of ethical gameplay, that is, the decision is one-off and irreversible.

Title: Outlining a Serious Moral Games in Bioethics
Snippet: Up to recently, the general relationship between morality and video games was considered from a limited perspective. It was (and is) common to debate whether certain games (such as first-person shooters) have a negative impact on the moral development of adolescents [8], although the findings are controversial [9]. 

We will not comment on this debate here, but we remark that an increasing interest in creating "pro-social" video games has shown up in several ways. Some authors strongly maintain that video games -in contrast to other instruments of moral education like stories or films -are particularly well suited for such purposes in that such games do not merely convey content; rather, the rules on which the games are based allow the player to act (within the established framework of the game) [10], and thus interact, rather than simply absorb. This use of video games is accompanied by a noteworthy development in the game industry. There have been for some time games on the market in which the player has to develop explicitly moral qualities (e.g. cooperation) to succeed. The associated "socially conscious artificial intelligence" aspect of a game engine has become quite common in game design. Examples of such behaviours include taking responsibility or feeling empathy for game characters, and a game flow that responds to the behaviour of the players (e.g. assertive versus cautious) [11]. However, the possibility of moral decisions in such games is not usually discussed in terms of their possible realization in a video game, but in the context of cultural analysis [12]. 

Nevertheless, this discussion points to the possibility of creating a SMG: a game that enables one to determine the "morality" of players, and possibly have an effect on their behaviour outside of the game world as well. Naturally this goal raises methodical questions, whose answers form the prerequisites for such a project: 

1. What does one mean by the idea of "morality"? In a general sense, "morality" describes the social norms and values that constitute the standard for "morally correct behaviour". But: What sort of norm is "moral"? To what extent are such norms bound to cultural and historical frameworks? What modes of justification do moral norms require? 2. What model of moral agency should apply?

Title: Game Characters as Narrative Devices. A Comparative Analysis of Dragon Age: Origins and Mass Effect 2
Snippet: This article presents a comparative analysis of how characters are used as narrative tools in Bioware’s computer role-playing games Dragon Age: Origins (2009) and Mass Effect 2 (2010). The analysis aims to demonstrate how sophisticated narrative features can be integrated in gameplay through the development of interesting characters. Using a comparative analysis, the author shows that the two games’ have different approaches to using characters as narrative tools within the same genre, while also incorporating these narrative features tightly into gameplay. Central to the argument is the idea that presenting the player as protagonist is not necessarily the most fruitful approach to narrative experiences in games, and that narrative coherence may be better established and maintained through letting non-player characters carry the weight of narrative progression.

Title: There Is No Solution!: “Wicked Problems” in Digital Games
Snippet: Semi-wicked problems. The second form of wicked problems are semi-(or pseudo-) wicked problems. Semi-wicked problems do inspire narratological-ethical behavior in the gamer (rather than ludostrategic behavior), but the problem itself can be solved relatively easily by exploiting the game's saving/loading system. The player is able to empirically explore all the (unforeseen) consequences of all possible solutions within the game. This works especially well with explicit morality systems with short-term consequences. The moral problem is real on the level of the narrative but has no consequences on the ludological level. 

This kind of wicked problem occurs, for example, numerous times in the Mass Effects series, a series that has been the subject of scholarly research concerning ethical gameplay before (Boyan, 2015;Knoll, 2015). The games in the Mass Effect series, which consists of three interconnected games, can be characterized as secondperson (over-the-shoulder), action role-playing games. All three installments (released in 2007, 2010, and 2012) were produced by BioWare. Moral choices made in the first (and the second) game are transferred to the second (and third) installment, creating an interlinked narratological and ludological unity. The series is set within the near future (end of the 22nd century), where interstellar travel is possible through a network of Mass Relays. The relays were built by a now extinct alien race known as the Protheans. 

With the help of Prothean technology discovered on Mars, humankind takes a decisive step into the galactic arena, where there are many sentinel and spacetraveling races. The Milky Way is governed by a conglomerate body known as the Citadel Council, which is dominated by the three most powerful races in our galaxy, Asari, Salarians, and Turians, later also joined by humanity. The player's moral behavior is explicitly recorded and evaluated by means of two morality meters, "paragon" (good) and "renegade" (evil), as I described earlier in this article. 

In the three game installments, the player gathers multiple teammates from different in-game races who can be chosen by the player to accompany him on missions.

Title: ‘Instant Karma’—Moral Decision Making Systems in Digital Games
Snippet: A Shepard with a focus on "Paragon" points and decisions tends to bring more companions and above all himself through the last mission. 

What may already become clear here is a slight tendency of the developers to prefer or reward the path of the "Paragon", at least in the narrative aspects of the game. Although it is also possible to save your team and yourself by focusing on "Renegade" points, it is often necessary to use "Paragon" conversation options to establish the necessary personal ties to the team members. This also illustrates the image that Bioware itself draws of the two ideal types of "Paragon" and "Renegade" and which is summarized as follows in the Mass Effect Wiki: Paragon points are gained for compassionate and heroic actions. [ . . . ] Points are often gained when asking about feelings and motivations of characters. The conversation options that lead to better understanding and thus loyalty on the part of the teammates will therefore in most cases be the "Paragon" options. 

However, the "karma system" of Mass Effect 2 influences the narrative structures of the game on another level, which is perhaps less obvious. The sheer existence of this system alone often puts action and missions-both main and sub missions-into a framework that leads to decisions between two options from which the player must choose. However, the "karma system" of Mass Effect 2 only knows two values, namely "Paragon" and "Renegade", which, simply through their presentation in dialogues, the presentation in the character view, as well as through aesthetic aspects, almost impose the image of two moral spectra to be understood as contradictory. Accordingly, each such decision must be assigned a moral value, which contradicts the principle of moral dilemmas actually pursued by the developers. 

A good example of how the "karma system" can also superimpose narrative structures and principles is provided by Daniel Floyd, owner of the Youtube Channel Extra Credits20 . He refers to a situation in Mass Effect 2 where the player has to decide whether he should wipe out or reprogram a species of artificial intelligences that are hostile to humans and have developed their own consciousness. In the game, the wiping is rewarded with "Renegade" and the reprogramming with "Paragon" points. Floyd comments on this:

Title: ‘Instant Karma’—Moral Decision Making Systems in Digital Games
Snippet: If we look at this in the context of Mass Effect 2, it may explain why, despite the developers' attempt to move away from a pure 'good/evil' dichotomy, a clearly oriented moral attitude has stronger effects and is therefore more desirable for the player than a 'balanced' way of playing. Semi-wicked problems. The second form of wicked problems are semi-(or pseudo-) wicked problems. Semi-wicked problems do inspire narratological-ethical behavior in the gamer (rather than ludostrategic behavior), but the problem itself can be solved relatively easily by exploiting the game's saving/loading system. The player is able to empirically explore all the (unforeseen) consequences of all possible solutions within the game. This works especially well with explicit morality systems with short-term consequences. The moral problem is real on the level of the narrative but has no consequences on the ludological level. 

This kind of wicked problem occurs, for example, numerous times in the Mass Effects series, a series that has been the subject of scholarly research concerning ethical gameplay before (Boyan, 2015;Knoll, 2015). The games in the Mass Effect series, which consists of three interconnected games, can be characterized as secondperson (over-the-shoulder), action role-playing games. All three installments (released in 2007, 2010, and 2012) were produced by BioWare. Moral choices made in the first (and the second) game are transferred to the second (and third) installment, creating an interlinked narratological and ludological unity. The series is set within the near future (end of the 22nd century), where interstellar travel is possible through a network of Mass Relays. The relays were built by a now extinct alien race known as the Protheans. 

With the help of Prothean technology discovered on Mars, humankind takes a decisive step into the galactic arena, where there are many sentinel and spacetraveling races. The Milky Way is governed by a conglomerate body known as the Citadel Council, which is dominated by the three most powerful races in our galaxy, Asari, Salarians, and Turians, later also joined by humanity. The player's moral behavior is explicitly recorded and evaluated by means of two morality meters, "paragon" (good) and "renegade" (evil), as I described earlier in this article. 

In the three game installments, the player gathers multiple teammates from different in-game races who can be chosen by the player to accompany him on missions.

A Shepard with a focus on "Paragon" points and decisions tends to bring more companions and above all himself through the last mission. 

What may already become clear here is a slight tendency of the developers to prefer or reward the path of the "Paragon", at least in the narrative aspects of the game. This also illustrates the image that Bioware itself draws of the two ideal types of "Paragon" and "Renegade" and which is summarized as follows in the Mass Effect Wiki: Paragon points are gained for compassionate and heroic actions. [ . . . ] Points are often gained when asking about feelings and motivations of characters. The conversation options that lead to better understanding and thus loyalty on the part of the teammates will therefore in most cases be the "Paragon" options.

However, the "karma system" of Mass Effect 2 only knows two values, namely "Paragon" and "Renegade", which, simply through their presentation in dialogues, the presentation in the character view, as well as through aesthetic aspects, almost impose the image of two moral spectra to be understood as contradictory. Accordingly, each such decision must be assigned a moral value, which contradicts the principle of moral dilemmas actually pursued by the developers.

Summary answer
Maintaining functional consistency does not inherently require sacrificing emergent narrative; instead, it imposes a design constraint that, if poorly implemented, can stifle openness, but with careful architecture and authoring it can coexist with emergent player-driven storytelling. Systems that dynamically align NPC behavior with evolving world state, enforce high-level constraints via validation, and use personality models show that character coherence can remain intact while preserving space for emergent plot and interaction. The core risks—content homogeneity, brittle filtering, and over-constraint—have recognized mitigations (author-specified structures, story graphs/behavior trees, and hybrid storylet-plus-LLM frameworks), and reputation/relationship mechanics demonstrate scalable ways to let consistent character identity shape emergent outcomes without locking out player agency. <cite id="0956e99c-0">Players form expectations of NPCs from the coherence and consistency of appearance and behavior, and these expectations support immersion and predictive engagement</cite><cite id="0956e99c-1">Dynamic, prompt-updated role-playing models can maintain alignment with character traits, background, and current narrative context while sustaining open-world responsiveness</cite><cite id="0956e99c-2">Validation-based generative pipelines inject high-level narrative criteria and enforce rules to align free-form interactions with the game’s story and character consistency</cite><cite id="0956e99c-4">Psychological models like the Big Five used for NPC personality yield more nuanced interactions and increased player engagement</cite><cite id="47bf9181-0">Emergent narrative systems built from minimal specifications can suffer homogeneity and limited authorial control unless augmented with structures that constrain at the right granularity</cite><cite id="47bf9181-3">Hybrid designs (e.g., story graphs plus dynamic revision, LLM-driven character simulation within abstract-act structures, or storylet hybrids) preserve coherence while remaining responsive to player input</cite><cite id="d6354351-0">Reputation/karma systems measure a character’s relationship with the world and can modulate narrative and ludic consequences without abolishing choice</cite><cite id="d6354351-1">Alignment systems with purely ludic penalties can undermine roleplay; the most memorable decisions are narrative-driven rather than consequence-driven</cite>.

Definitions and stakes
- Character functional consistency refers to keeping a coherent persona, goals, and behavior patterns across time and contexts so players can form stable mental models and reliably predict interactions. <cite id="0956e99c-0">Players infer roles from the coherence between appearance and behavior and reinforce expectations via consistency over time; this improves immersion and decision-making by anchoring behavior in a coherent world</cite>.
- Emergent narrative arises when system-level rules and agent interactions yield unplanned stories in response to player agency, often in open-world or persistent environments. <cite id="47bf9181-1">Simulation-based (emergent) systems let characters act from decentralized agent behavior, while deliberative planners solve for constrained optimal actions; both approaches face risks when goals/world facts misalign, producing short or odd narratives</cite><cite id="0956e99c-3">Modular/adaptive, procedurally generated narration supports nonlinear, player-influenced plots and unique interactive experiences</cite>.

Why naive consistency threatens emergence
- Minimalist, free-form generative systems demonstrate the baseline tension: using only high-level world/character specs can yield coherent stories at runtime but often with limited authorial control and homogeneity, and agent-based emergent behavior may drift outside intended social norms and character bounds. <cite id="47bf9181-0">Interactive emergent systems like AI Dungeon generate dialogues/behaviors entirely at runtime from minimal specs; they reduce authoring burden but suffer content homogeneity and limited control, while agent-based frameworks show unpredictability without strong affordances for shaping character behavior</cite>.
- Without guardrails, emergent behaviors can violate coherence or consistency. <cite id="47bf9181-1">When character goals or world facts misalign with user intent, simulation-based systems can produce short, oddly structured narratives</cite>. Even when systems add high-level outlines, rigidity can hinder adaptation to player input, narrowing emergent space. <cite id="47bf9181-0">Hierarchical decompositions provide high-level structural control but can be brittle to player input, often deployed as end-to-end generators rather than responsive interactive stories</cite>.
- Reputation and morality mechanics illustrate that global “alignment” knobs can scale consistency, but if misapplied, they can trivialize choice or impose heavy-handed penalties. <cite id="d6354351-4">Bipolar morality scales move a character along good/evil and lawful/chaotic axes to trigger consequences in narrative and gameplay; they scale authoring but can be used as narrative or ludic mechanics</cite><cite id="d6354351-1">Engaging decisions often overwhelm specific ludic consequences; alignment systems with purely punitive or additive effects can be counterproductive to roleplay</cite>.

Architectures that preserve consistency while enabling emergence
- Personality- and psychology-driven models for NPCs. <cite id="0956e99c-4">Using models like the Big Five to parameterize NPC traits yields more nuanced, human-like, and dynamic responses to social stimuli, increasing engagement</cite>. These models can be embedded in “personality-biased” NPCs that guide dialogue and action without determinism, allowing emergent variation within a coherent type space. <cite id="0956e99c-2">A procedural narrative framework injects high-level criteria and validates generated content against rules, aligning free-form player interactions with the narrative and maintaining consistency</cite>.
- Dynamic authorship and validation. <cite id="0956e99c-1">Role-playing prompts that are continuously updated with static traits, task info, and current narrative context sustain alignment with character backgrounds while remaining responsive to evolving plots in open worlds</cite>. <cite id="0956e99c-2">Validation systems parse designer criteria into gameplay rules and iteratively refine LLM outputs during play to preserve coherence with the procedural narrative</cite>. <cite id="47bf9181-3">Hybrid systems combine LLM-driven character simulation with abstract-act authorial structures to co-author dynamic plots and bound emergent behaviors to maintain coherence under player interaction</cite>.

Title: Breaking Players’ Expectations: The Role of Non-Player Characters’ Coherence and Consistency
Snippet: N video games, human players control a main character who interacts with non-player characters (NPCs) who populate the game. NPCs are designed with specific characteristics, chosen by game designers, that communicate their role in the narrative. NPCs can play different roles, such as allies or enemies. Game designers often use two characteristics to communicate NPCs' roles in the narrative: appearance and behaviors [1]. Players then form expectations about the role of NPCs based on the perceived coherence between their appearance and their behaviors [2]. Coherence refers to the correspondence between NPCs' features and players' stereotypes. It allows players to understand NPCs' behaviors within the wider context of the game world [3]. Players' expectations are reinforced by the consistency of NPCs' design throughout the game [4]. Consistency refers to the design parameters' alignment, such as appearance and behaviors, over time. It allows players to form expectations and ensure that NPCs' actions match predefined visual cues, in order to convey their role in the game [1]. For example, in a military shooter game, encountering an aggressive NPC who looks like a soldier influences the expectation of hostility when encountering a second NPC with a similar appearance. If the second soldier encountered confirms players' expectations, this will make it easier to predict hostility in subsequent encounters. The aim of maintaining both consistency and coherence between appearance and behaviors is to allow players to form accurate expectations of enemies or allies and, as a result, to improve the overall experience of the game [5]. In particular, when NPCs' behaviors match their appearance and fit logically into the game world, players can better immerse themselves in the narrative and make informed decisions throughout the game. 

As part of their immersion, players form impressions of the NPCs based on their appearance and behaviors [6]. When interacting with NPCs, players assess their perceived intelligence and believability. Perceived intelligence is defined as the player's evaluation of NPCs' abilities to achieve their objective in the narrative, encompassing two dimensions: behaviors' understandability and performance [7].

Snippet: Narrative generation systems can often be classified as using one of two approaches to fictional fabula content creation. Simulation-based narrative generation systems (also referred to as emergent systems in Aylett, 1999Aylett, , 2000 are those that simulate a story world. The simulation approach is to establish a set of characters and a world context. The narrative generation system then progressively determines the actions that the characters should take over time as the situational context evolves. Often simulation-based narrative generation systems employ decentralized, autonomous embodied agents that represent story world characters and react to the evolving world state. Deliberative narrative generation systems are those that generate narratives by solving the problem of choosing a sequence of actionsphysical, mental, and dialogue -for all story world characters that meet certain constraints and parameters (aesthetic, dramatic, or pedagogical). The narrative is the output of this procedure.
